    • Support and resistance

    Breaker block: an OB that was closed through and switched roles

    A breaker block is an order block that price closed through, which invalidated it. When price later comes back, the broken zone can work in the opposite direction. A broken bearish OB becomes a bullish breaker, a broken bullish OB a bearish breaker.

    What is a breaker block?

    An order block (OB) does not always hold. Price comes back to the zone and this time closes beyond its far end. The OB is invalidated. This broken zone is called a breaker block.

    A breaker is read through role reversal: an area that was supply can work as demand once price is above it; an area that was demand can work as supply once price is below it.

    The term breaker also comes from the "Smart Money Concepts" approach. This page treats it as a measurable closing and structure rule.

    Directions

    • Bullish breaker: a bearish OB that price passed with a close above its high. When price later comes back to it from above, the zone can work as support.
    • Bearish breaker: a bullish OB that price passed with a close below its low. When price later comes back to it from below, the zone can work as resistance.

    How does it form?

    Each step gives the bullish breaker first, then the bearish breaker.

    1. An OB forms A sharp move that breaks structure leaves an OB. For a bullish breaker this is the last up candle before a drop that broke structure down, a bearish OB. For a bearish breaker it is the last down candle before a rise that broke structure up, a bullish OB.
    2. Price closes through the OB Price comes back to the zone and closes above its high for a bullish breaker, below its low for a bearish breaker. A wick past the zone is not enough; the close decides.
    3. Structure breaks in the new direction If, after the break, a close comes above the previous high for a bullish breaker or below the previous low for a bearish breaker (BOS or CHoCH), the change of direction is confirmed by structure too. This step is not required, but it is the most important feature that strengthens a breaker.
    4. The zone is watched the other way The zone is extended to the right. When price comes back to it, from above for a bullish breaker and from below for a bearish breaker, its behaviour there is watched.

    What makes a breaker stronger

    • The broken zone was a valid OB that met the rules.
    • Price passed the zone without resistance, with one or two strong candles; it did not linger there.
    • After the break, structure broke in the new direction (BOS or CHoCH).
    • It is the first return to the zone. Each new test can weaken its effect.
    • The zone is close to an important support or resistance area on a larger timeframe.

    A common explanation: those who traded from the OB are at a loss once the zone breaks, and may close their positions when price returns to their entry. This is an explanation, not proof.

    When price comes back to the breaker

    When price returns to a breaker, one of three pictures usually follows. Each card gives the bullish breaker first, then the bearish breaker.

    Role reversal holds

    Price enters the zone, closes stay inside it and price moves in the new direction; it rises from a bullish breaker and falls from a bearish breaker.

    Weak reaction

    Price lingers in the zone and the move in the new direction stays short. The zone shows neither its old nor its new role clearly.

    Breaker invalidated

    A candle closes beyond the far end of the zone; below the low for a bullish breaker, above the high for a bearish breaker. The role reversal did not hold and the zone loses most of its meaning.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • That an OB was closed through and invalidated
    • That the broken zone is an opposite-direction area to watch when price comes back
    • Whether the role reversal is backed by a break of structure

    What it does not prove

    • That price must come back to the zone
    • That the zone must hold in its new role
    • That a particular group of buyers or sellers is waiting at a loss in the zone

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    MarketLevelMap's charts do not draw breakers separately, but how they are read can be followed with the marks on the page.

    • The CHoCH label in the Price Action view shows where structure changed direction. A breaker often forms near such a change of direction.
    • On the Critical Zones charts a resistance zone that price moved above can show up as a support zone, and a support zone that price moved below as a resistance zone. This is the wider-zone counterpart of a breaker's role reversal.

    Timeframes

    On small timeframes OBs are broken often, so breakers form often too and most are short-lived. A breaker on a larger timeframe covers a wider area and can be watched for longer. A breaker is read together with the timeframe it was marked on.

    Often confused with

    • Order block (OB): the last opposite candle before a sharp moveAn OB is the last opposite candle before a sharp move and is expected to work in its own direction; a breaker is an OB that was closed through and works in the opposite direction.
    • Retests and role reversal: returning to a broken zoneRole reversal can happen at any support or resistance zone; a breaker applies that idea to the zone that comes from a single OB candle.
    • False breakout: the wick versus the closeIn a false breakout price moves past the zone but the close comes back on the old side; with a breaker the close comes on the other side of the zone and price stays there.

    Key points

    • A breaker is an OB that was closed through and invalidated.
    • A broken bearish OB becomes a bullish breaker, a broken bullish OB a bearish breaker.
    • A break of structure in the new direction after the break strengthens a breaker.
    • There is no guarantee that the zone will hold in its new role.
